clinicalPearls: A malignant melanocytic tumour of the conjunctiva presenting as a variably pigmented, often nodular and vascularised lesion, though amelanotic forms occur
Most cases arise from primary acquired melanosis with atypia; a minority arise from a pre-existing naevus or de novo
Primary acquired melanosis appears as flat, patchy, acquired conjunctival pigmentation in middle-aged and older patients and must be assessed for atypia
Location beyond the bulbar conjunctiva (palpebral, forniceal, caruncular, or tarsal) and thicker tumours carry a worse prognosis
Diagnosis relies on excisional biopsy with a no-touch technique; incomplete or incisional biopsy of the primary tumour is discouraged where excision is feasible
Management combines wide local excision with adjunctive cryotherapy to the margins, with topical chemotherapy for diffuse primary acquired melanosis and map biopsies to define extent
Regional (preauricular and cervical) nodes are the first site of metastatic spread, so nodal assessment and sometimes sentinel node biopsy are relevant
reference.pathophysiology: Conjunctival melanoma is a malignant proliferation of conjunctival melanocytes. The commonest precursor is primary acquired melanosis with atypia, an acquired intraepithelial melanocytic proliferation in which increasing atypia predicts transformation to invasive melanoma; less often the tumour develops from a pre-existing conjunctival naevus or arises de novo. Ultraviolet exposure and characteristic driver mutations contribute to melanocytic transformation. Malignant melanocytes proliferate within and beneath the conjunctival epithelium, and invasive disease can spread through conjunctival lymphatics to regional preauricular and cervical nodes and thereafter haematogenously; extrabulbar sites and greater tumour thickness are associated with higher risks of recurrence and metastasis.
additionalDifferentials: Ocular surface squamous neoplasia (especially pigmented or amelanotic overlap)
Conjunctival pigmented pyogenic granuloma or foreign-body pigmentation
Extension of uveal melanoma or ciliary body tumour
additionalInvestigations: Detailed slit-lamp examination mapping pigmentation, nodularity, and feeder vessels
Excisional biopsy with a no-touch technique and adjunctive cryotherapy
Map (multiple conjunctival) biopsies to delineate primary acquired melanosis extent
Histopathology with assessment of thickness, invasion, and margins
Regional lymph node examination and imaging, with sentinel node biopsy in selected cases
Systemic staging imaging for higher-risk or recurrent tumours
redFlags: New nodularity, rapid growth, or increasing vascularity within an area of conjunctival pigmentation
Extrabulbar involvement of the fornix, palpebral conjunctiva, caruncle, or tarsus
Recurrence after treatment or extensive diffuse primary acquired melanosis with atypia
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on tumour thickness, location, and completeness of excision; bulbar limbal tumours that are thin and completely excised fare better, whereas extrabulbar, thick, or recurrent tumours carry a substantial risk of local recurrence and regional or distant metastasis with corresponding mortality.
pitfalls: Dismissing acquired flat conjunctival pigmentation without assessing primary acquired melanosis for atypia
Performing incisional biopsy or non-excisional manipulation of a resectable primary tumour
Omitting adjunctive cryotherapy and map biopsies, increasing recurrence and missing diffuse disease
Overlooking amelanotic melanoma and mistaking it for squamous neoplasia or a benign lesion
management: Localized bulbar disease is treated with curative intent via complete surgical excision aiming for clear margins in a single procedure

Extrabulbar or diffuse disease (palpebral, forniceal, caruncular, or tarsal involvement, or diffuse primary acquired melanosis with atypia) is treated with combined surgery and topical or radiation therapy with closer surveillance
Resectable regional nodal disease is treated with curative intent via surgical clearance of the involved nodal basin, with consideration of adjuvant radiotherapy
Metastatic disease shifts intent to systemic disease control and is referred to medical oncology and managed as systemic melanoma
Wide local excision using a no touch technique is the standard primary surgical approach to avoid tumor seeding
Incisional or partial biopsy of a resectable primary lesion is discouraged in favor of excising the whole lesion for accurate margin assessment
Map biopsies are used for diffuse primary acquired melanosis with atypia to define the extent of atypical melanocytic change
Adjunctive cryotherapy is applied to surgical margins after excision to reduce local recurrence
Regional lymph node assessment is part of staging, with sentinel lymph node biopsy used selectively in thicker or higher risk tumors
Adjuvant radiotherapy, using plaque brachytherapy or proton beam radiotherapy, is added for thick tumors, close or involved margins, or local recurrence, rather than as primary treatment
Topical chemotherapy with an agent such as mitomycin C is used for diffuse primary acquired melanosis with atypia, either after excision or for extensive atypical change not amenable to excision

Confirmed metastatic or unresectable regional disease is managed with systemic therapy, with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy referenced for metastatic disease and specific regimen selection left to medical oncology
There is no established role for cytotoxic chemotherapy as primary treatment of localized conjunctival melanoma

Lifelong monitoring includes slit lamp surveillance for recurrence and new primary acquired melanosis, regional lymph node examination, and periodic systemic staging imaging in higher risk or recurrent tumors, with referral to ophthalmic oncology for nodularity, rapid growth, extrabulbar extension, lymphadenopathy, recurrence, or metastatic disease
